reasoning_summary: Step-by-step: 0005 fixes two perfect matchings M, M' of the tree T=(V,E) -- legitimate, since 'at most one' is proved by showing any two coincide. 0006 forms the spanning subgraph G on V whose edges are the matching edges of M and M'. Since M and M' are matchings, every vertex has exactly one M-edge and exactly one M'-edge, so every vertex of G has degree 1 (when the two edges coincide) or 2 (when they differ); consequently every component of G is either a single shared edge or a cycle whose edges alternate between M and M', and no component can be a path of length >= 2. A tree has no cycles, and G is a subgraph of T, so no cyclic component can occur; hence every component is a single edge lying in both M and M', i.e. M = M'. The write-up's only defect is a wording slip: with edge set M u M' the degenerate components are shared edges, not 'isolated vertices' (isolated vertices are the degenerate components of the symmetric difference M \Delta M', the other standard formulation of the same argument, and the author's parenthetical 'which is in M and M'' shows that is the intended reading). Under either formulation the stated dichotomy and the conclusion M = M' are correct, so this is an expositional imprecision rather than a logical gap; the proof's structure and every load-bearing inference are sound.
